notable_claims: UK academic institutions operating news servers often decided not to forward the 'alt.*' hierarchy of Usenet.
The University of Delaware faculty senate adopted a 'Policy for Responsible Computing' acknowledging legal obligations regarding copyrights and security in electronic media.
Senator Byrd sponsored a bill to rescind peer-reviewed NSF grants that had 'funny names' as a political statement against pork barrel spending.
classification.summary: This is a digest abstract summarizing ten items related to academic freedom and computing. Key topics include the University of Delaware's 'Policy for Responsible Computing,' UK academic institutions filtering Usenet 'alt.*' hierarchies, and Senator Byrd's attempt to rescind NSF grants based on their names.
classification.title: Abstract of CAF-News 02.25

notable_claims: The University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee assistant chancellor for student affairs stated the right to display the banner was protected under the First Amendment.
classification.summary: A UPI news report describes a physical altercation at the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee after a man tore down a banner depicting a swastika evolving into a Star of David. The banner had been placed by Palestinian students with university permission. A university official stated that the display was protected under the First Amendment.
classification.title: Banner prompts fight at university

notable_claims: The university's sign-posting policy required prior approval and prohibited content deemed obscene or sexist.
The ACLU claims administrators cannot interfere with First Amendment rights unless expression disrupts school work, discipline, or the rights of others.
classification.summary: The Young Conservatives of Texas sued Stephen F. Austin State University after the school banned signs featuring a quote by Barry Goldwater regarding sex and politics. The ACLU filed the suit, arguing that the university's sign-posting policy violated First Amendment rights. The university had deemed the content sexist and obscene.
classification.title: Students sue over sex sign ban

identity.subject: Article 2--[UPI] "Students sue over sex sign ban"

notable_claims: The Policy for Responsible Computing was approved by the full faculty senate on May 11, 1992.
Access to university computing facilities is defined as a privilege granted to students, faculty, and staff.
Violations of the policy may be prosecuted under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act of 1986 or Delaware Code.
classification.summary: Richard Gordon announces that the University of Delaware Faculty Senate approved a 'Policy for Responsible Computing' after five years of development. The policy establishes governing philosophies for the use of computing resources, emphasizing legal compliance and ethical standards. It defines access as a privilege and outlines enforcement mechanisms linked to university handbooks and federal law.
classification.title: Status of UDel's Responsible Computing Policy

identity.subject: Article 3--Re:  Status of UDel's Responsible Computing Policy

notable_claims: Senator Byrd sought to rescind NSF grants based on their titles to embarrass the administration.
The politicization of research grants leads to increased bureaucratic layers and delays in processing.
classification.summary: The post warns about a political effort led by Senator Robert Byrd to rescind funding for specific peer-reviewed NSF grants based on 'silly-sounding' titles. While computer science grants were not explicitly targeted in this instance, the author argues that politicizing research funding undermines the merit review process and creates bureaucratic delays. The message includes an action alert from the American Psychological Association urging scientists to protect the integrity of federal research funding.
classification.title: Article 4--From the Computing Research Association

notable_claims: The Harvard Law School disciplinary board found no rule limiting the content of student publications applicable to the parody article.
Professor David Kennedy claimed the parody was 'incompatible with an open academic environment.'
classification.summary: The Harvard Law School disciplinary board declined to take action against students who wrote a parody article titled 'Manifesto of Post-Mortem Legal Feminism.' The board stated that no existing law school rules imposed limits on the content of student publications. This followed calls for disciplinary action by Professor David Kennedy, who argued the work was incompatible with an open academic environment.
classification.title: Harvard Law School uproar update

classification.summary: William W. Arnold of the EFF provides technical instructions to a user on how to subscribe or unsubscribe from mailing lists via listserv@eff.org. The message includes a detailed guide on available commands and subscription management for the comp-academic-freedom-talk list.
classification.title: Article 6--Re: help

notable_claims: Publicly supported libraries are recognized as limited public forums for access to information.
Library policies restricting access must be based on objective behavior rather than subjective reactions or arbitrary classifications.
classification.summary: Richard F. Bennett shared draft guidelines from the ALA Intellectual Freedom Committee regarding patron behavior and library usage. The document outlines how libraries should balance the First Amendment right to receive information with the need to maintain a safe environment through reasonable restrictions on time, place, and manner of access.
classification.title: IFC Proposed Behavior Guidelines

notable_claims: Springfield, Oregon passed a proposal forbidding the promotion of homosexuality.
A City Councilor requested library acquisition lists to monitor content in the children's section.
The OCA sought a state ballot measure requiring teachers to teach that homosexuality is wrong.
classification.summary: The post reports on a proposal passed in Springfield, Oregon, intended to prevent the promotion of homosexuality and other behaviors. A City Councilor requested a list of recently ordered library books to ensure compliance with 'community values.' The Oregon Citizens Alliance (OCA) is also noted as attempting to mandate that teachers instruct students that homosexuality is wrong.
classification.title: OCA library censorship

notable_claims: Academic institutions in the UK frequently filtered 'alt.*' newsgroups to avoid public scandal.
Server operators exercised discretionary control over content forwarding based on perceived suitability.
classification.summary: A discussion regarding the filtering of Usenet newsgroups in the UK, specifically the 'alt.*' hierarchy and groups like alt.drugs. The author argues that academic institutions running servers choose not to forward this content to avoid negative press regarding the use of taxpayer funds. The post highlights the tension between server operators' discretion and users' expectations of access.
classification.title: Article 9--Re: Possible censorship

notable_claims: Real-time conferencing systems (RELAY/IRC) differ from email because one user's behavior can disrupt hundreds of others simultaneously.
The existence of an /ignore command reduces the need for administrators to remove user access.
Lack of persistent filtering tools (like KILL files) is a reason to improve software rather than institute censorship.
classification.summary: A discussion regarding the management of harassment and obscenity on BITNET RELAY, a real-time conferencing system. The participants debate whether administrators should act as regulators (similar to the FCC) or if technical solutions like /ignore commands are sufficient to prevent censorship.
classification.title: Article 10--Re: Restriction or not ?
